records.app_claim: "Rhodri became king of Gwynedd in 844, took Powys in 855 and Seisyllwg in 872, so that for a few years one king ruled most of Wales outside the south-east and Dyfed. He was killed fighting the English; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography gives 877, other reckonings 878. His sons divided the lands. No boundary is drawn because none is known."
records.research_claim: Thornton qualifies Rhodri’s control of Powys as possible in 855 or later; the app’s “took Powys in 855” is too definite. Death chronology remains 877 versus 878.
The scalar end 1063 should support an alternative 1064 end as already acknowledged in the app note. Store Hudson and Jones as competing chronology claims.

records.app_claim: "Hywel held Seisyllwg from 920 and Dyfed by marriage, and on the death of Idwal Foel in 942 took Gwynedd (and with it Powys), ruling all Wales except Morgannwg and Gwent until his death in 950. The Welsh law-books are attributed to him, though no manuscript is earlier than the 13th century. His kingdom broke up at his death."
records.research_claim: The statement that no law manuscript predates the thirteenth century conflicts with DWB’s late-twelfth-century earliest manuscript; attribution of the law collection to Hywel is not contemporary documentation.
867 is a display placeholder. English Heritage explicitly says abandonment occurred at an unknown point in the ninth century. Preserve a bounded uncertain end.
674 dates Wearmouth; Jarrow followed c.681–682 and was dedicated 23 April 685. Separate place/structure phases avoid making the Jarrow marker appear in 674.

records.app_claim: "Founded in 635 from Iona. Cuthbert died here in 687 and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made about 710-725. Raided on 8 June 793, left for good in 875, and refounded as a cell of Durham by 1122 until its closure in 1537."
records.research_claim: Cuthbert died on Farne, not at Lindisfarne. His burial was at Lindisfarne. The app’s “died here” conflates death and burial.
The archaeological camp is on the high ground north of Torksey, mostly Brampton parish, centred on HER grid SK836802. A village marker is not the camp centroid.

records.app_claim: "A Mercian royal mausoleum. The Great Army wintered here in 873-4, and a D-shaped earthwork and a mass grave of at least 264 people have been excavated."
records.research_claim: The minimum 264 individuals is supported by the published charnel study. It is a burial assemblage, not a count of deaths in a documented battle.
records.notes: Final author classification: cited evidence confirms or qualifies the already cautious app statement; this is not a demonstrated disagreement.

records.app_claim: "Roman Venta, refounded by Alfred with a new street grid and the largest burh in the Burghal Hidage. It was second only to London at Domesday but thirtieth in the 1377 poll tax."
records.research_claim: The Hidage assessment is 2,400 hides for Winchester, also 2,400 for Wallingford and appended Warwick. These fiscal figures do not by themselves establish an exclusive largest-town ranking or population.
The event is attested but this point is a candidate localization. The Chronicle does not identify a modern coordinate; render a disputed candidate, not a fixed battlefield.
Retain both Ashingdon/Canewdon and Ashdon/Hadstock hypotheses. The project still calls the location disputed; an Ashingdon marker must not become confirmed geometry.

records.app_claim: "Egbert of Wessex defeated Beornwulf of Mercia; Kent, Sussex, Surrey and Essex passed to Wessex and Mercian dominance ended."
records.research_claim: The Chronicle distinguishes Ecgberht’s victory, Æthelwulf’s subsequent expulsion of Baldred, and East Anglian resistance to Mercia. This is a campaign sequence, not a single instantaneous territorial switch.
Documentary attestation is a much later origin annal. The packet marks the event tradition/low, preserving the stated 577 date without presenting contemporary proof.
1014 is the saga framing, not a secure event date from the Chronicle. The Chronicle records repeated attacks in 1009–10 and Æthelred’s return in 1014, without bridge demolition.
Fraction 0.5 is staging. The attested timing is two nights after relief of London, after the Sherston encounter and before Assandun; no fixed day or month is recorded.
654 cannot mean the first existence of Northumbria as a united kingship: Edwin and Oswald ruled both components before it, with intervening divisions. Use successive polity phases.

records.app_claim: "The monastery founded by St David in the 6th century became the leading church of Wales and, under Norman bishops from 1115, a cathedral. The present church was begun in 1181; a 12th-century pope ruled two pilgrimages here equal to one to Rome, and Bishop Henry de Gower built the great palace in 1328-47."
records.research_claim: St Davids had bishops before Norman appointments: Nobis appears in the annals under 840 and Asser describes its bishops. Separate early episcopal institution from the later cathedral building.
